title: Final: inside the heap
cards/0/q: An object was used as a Dictionary key (its hash taken via the non-overridden GetHashCode), and then it is locked on. What happens to the header?
cards/0/options/0: The hash already occupies the header, so the CLR creates a sync block and writes its index into the header
cards/0/options/1: The thin lock overwrites the hash, and the key gets lost
cards/0/options/3: The hash is recomputed after leaving the lock
cards/0/explain: The 32 header bits hold only one thing: a thin lock, a hash or a sync block index. When both are needed, the hash and the monitor state move into a sync block, and the hash does not change.
cards/1/q: How many bytes does an object of this class take on x64?
cards/1/explain: Auto layout: Next (+0), Value (+8), Kind (+12). 13 bytes of fields → 16, plus 16 of bookkeeping — 32.
cards/1/wrong/1: That is what the source order would give: byte, a 7-byte gap, a reference, an int, a 4-byte gap. But the CLR reorders class fields.
cards/2/q: Put the parts of new int[4] in order from the lowest address to the highest (x64)
cards/2/explain: The header is at ref − 8, the type pointer at the reference address, then the length padded to 8 bytes and the elements back to back. 24 + 16 = 40 bytes in total.
cards/3/q: What goes straight to the LOH? Select all.
cards/3/explain: double[11,000] is 88,024 bytes, a 45,000-character string is 90,022, object[12,000] is 96,024. char[40,000] and Guid[5,000] are 80,024 bytes each, below the 85,000 threshold.
cards/4/explain: A reference inside a struct switches it to auto layout: B (+0), A (+8), C (+9), rounded to 16. Sequential with gaps would give 24.
cards/4/wrong/1: That is what sequential layout would give. But with a reference inside, the CLR lays the struct out like a class.
cards/5/q: Match the term to its meaning
cards/5/pairs/0/1: An entry in a separate table for the hash and the monitor
cards/5/pairs/1/1: Where the references sit inside an object
cards/5/pairs/2/1: The size of an array element or a string character
cards/5/pairs/3/1: A heap block that belongs to one generation
cards/5/pairs/4/1: Literals and typeof results that are never collected
cards/6/q: Allocate a long-lived buffer for native I/O that will never move
cards/6/explain: pinned: true puts the array in the POH — objects there do not move, need no pinning and do not get in the way of SOH compaction.
cards/7/q: What changed in the heap with the move to regions in .NET 7?
cards/7/options/0: The heap is split into small regions that can pass between generations and go back to the OS one by one
cards/7/options/1: The LOH threshold grew to 4 MB
cards/7/options/2: The collector stopped dividing objects into generations
cards/7/options/3: Objects in the SOH no longer move
cards/7/explain: Generations, the LOH threshold and compaction stayed. The physical structure changed: instead of large segments, regions of 4 MB (32 MB for the LOH and POH) that move flexibly between generations.
cards/8/q: Library v2 reordered the fields of a public struct without references. The app writes it to a file as bytes via MemoryMarshal. What breaks?
cards/8/options/0: Reading files written by v1: the byte order is part of the format
cards/8/options/1: Nothing: the CLR computes offsets at load time
cards/8/explain: For access from IL the reordering is safe — offsets are computed at load time. But a struct without references has sequential layout, and its bytes in the file follow the field order.
